newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Defence attacks expert testimony on Rwanda genocide.
newsitem.headline: Defence attacks expert testimony on Rwanda genocide.

text.p: A prosecution witness testifying against a Hutu militia leader accused of genocide in the 1994 slaughter of Tutsis in Rwanda on Wednesday told the U.N. court that he did not find any traces of bones in a school compound where a massacre allegedly took place.

Pierre Heuts, a Dutch policeman who conducted an investigation for the prosecution, said under questioning by the defence that he had received most of his information from the director of the technical school during a visit in 1996.

But when defence lawyer Tiphaine Dickson of Canada asked Heuts whether the site had been preserved or protected over the two years, the policeman said he did not know because the soldiers at the school did not speak English.
"Normally, I wouldn't do a crime scene investigation after two years," said Heuts.
Heuts said he did not find any bodies buried at the school compound, nor did he find any traces of bones, although he identified powder from a hand grenade but had not sent it for analysis.

After the takeover of Rwanda by the Tutsi-dominated rebel Rwanda Patriotic Front, which siezed power in July 1994, putting an end to the three-month slaughter, bodies were removed from massacre sites. Only the remains of bodies at government-designated memorial massacre sites were left where the people were killed.
The prosecution plans to call a total of 35 witnesses in its case against Georges Rutaganda, who is being tried at the U.N. tribunal set up in Arusha, Tanzania, to hear cases of alleged genocide.
The defence team has said it would try and establish whether in fact a genocide took place or whether the Hutu majority was trying to defend itself against Tutsi rebels.
Rutaganda, 39, was vice-president of the Hutu Interahamwe militia, which was held responsible for massacres during the slaughter of about 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically-moderate Hutus.

Among other things, Rutaganda is accused of arming Hutu extremists in April 1994 and ordering the murder of Tutsi civilians with machetes, guns, grenades and drowning. The prosecution alleges that some victims were forced to dig their own graves.
Rutaganda, a former agricultural engineer and businessman, was charged last May with eight counts of genocide along with other crimes against humanity.
He has pleaded not guilty to all charges and his lawyers have said Rutaganda was a simple businessman and his position as a vice-president of the Interahamwe only a formal post and nothing more.
Under the rules of the U.N.'s Rwanda tribunal, Rutaganda faces life imprisonment if found guilty.
